newsitem.title: INDIA: India stocks seen consolidating after rally.
newsitem.headline: India stocks seen consolidating after rally.

text.p: Indian blue chips enter the week sitting on strong gains and analysts expect a phase of consolidation ahead of an impending rise in domestic petroleum product prices.
"The markets are due for some consolidation at current levels after the decent run we have seen," Nand Kishore Gupta, chief executive at Ind-Sec Share & Stock Brokers, told Reuters.
Bombay's widely tracked 30-share index surged 130 points or 3.50 percent last week, courtesy of a rally over the first four days before profit taking kicked in on Friday.
Renewed fund buying in multinationals, the oil and refinery sector and financial institutions drove the markets higher last week, with local players jumping onto the buying bandwagon, traders said.

"The market could move up decisively after the petroleum product price increases are announced, especially if the government raises the prices of subsidised petroleum products more than for other products," said Pravin Shah, analyst at Morgan Stanley.
Oil and refinery shares have provided a defensive hedge against the negative influence of petroleum product prices on Indian stocks markets, analysts said.
Some brokers said multinationals, like Hindustan Lever, Colgate and Nestle were at the top of funds' shopping lists.
"The spotlight is on multinational companies which are seen as growth stocks by foreign funds," said Vidyut Devendra Kumar, a member-broker of the Bombay Stock Exchange.
But Ind-Sec's Gupta said although he expected fund buying to continue, much of the inflow did not come from long-term investors.
"The market has seen a lot of money coming in from hedge funds. Basically, this is 'hot' money," Gupta said.
Analysts expect some profit-taking and a sense of caution ahead of the long-overdue increase in government-set oil prices.

"We may see a slightly downward focus next week, with sectors that are directly affected by the oil price hike like auto shares under pressure," said Aspi Contractor, head of research at Ceat Financial Services.
The 15-party ruling United Front government's policy-setting steering committee is expected to tackle oil prices on June 15.
Strong opposition from left-wing members of the coalition has held up earlier efforts to reach a consensus.

In the meantime, oil companies have waited for the government to repay them for shouldering the burden of India's complex subsidy system. The companies were owed 155 billion rupees ($4.33 billion) at the end of March, and the bill was rising.
The lack of action has dampened markets, with uncertainty over the timing of the price rise capping fresh demand, analysts said.
"The petrol price news is bound to have a temporary reaction," said Ind-Sec's Gupta. "But, if the hike does not come, it will be taken very badly by investors."
"This will show the government's inclination to comply with the populist forces and not with the market requirements."
